title: The God who sees (Genesis 16)
hook: Hagar, a runaway slave, gives God a name

segments.voice: Yesterday, count the stars, amen: an old man told to look up, and he believed. Your line was so shall thy seed be. Did you look up last night? Today, someone in the same household nobody looks at. Day three hundred forty-eight.

Abram and Sarai have lived ten years in Canaan, still with no child, and Sarai has stopped waiting. She takes matters into her own hands: she gives her Egyptian slave, a young woman named Hagar, to Abram, so a child can be born on her behalf. Hagar conceives. And the household cracks. Hagar looks down on Sarai; Sarai treats her harshly; Abram says, she's your slave, do what you like. So Hagar runs. Pregnant, alone, into the desert, on the road toward Egypt. Nobody comes after her. Nobody in the camp, anyway.
screen: `A SLAVE GIVEN TO ABRAM.` → `THE HOUSEHOLD CRACKS.` → `HAGAR RUNS INTO THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: First, the finding. By a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur, the angel of the Lord finds her. And notice the first thing said to her. In the Douay-Rheims: "Agar, handmaid of Sarai, whence comest thou? and whither goest thou?" Agar is the old spelling of Hagar. Two things here. The angel calls her by name. In this chapter, Abram and Sarai never once say her name; she's my handmaid, your handmaid. And the angel asks her questions, as if her answer matters. Second, the hard part. The angel tells her to go back and submit to Sarai. The text doesn't soften that, and we shouldn't either. But with it comes a promise: her descendants will be too many to count, and her son will be named Ishmael, which means God hears, because the Lord has heard her affliction. Third, the name. And then Hagar does something remarkable: she gives God a name. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thou the God who hast seen me." In Hebrew, El Roi, the God who sees. Not Abram. Not a priest. An Egyptian slave woman, pregnant, on the run, by a well in the desert. The well itself is named after it. Fourth, why it lasts. Catholic social teaching speaks of a God who hears the cry of the poor and sees the overlooked. Readers find that God here, by a spring in the desert. The person with the least power in the camp is the one who says who God is to her.
screen: `FOUND BY A SPRING, CALLED BY NAME.` · `GO BACK: THE TEXT DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` · `ISHMAEL: GOD HEARS.` · `EL ROI: SHE NAMES GOD.` · then, large: `THOU THE GOD WHO HAST SEEN ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice someone overlooked. Settle, and breathe. Think back through yesterday. Who was there that you didn't really see? The cashier. The cleaner leaving the office as you arrived. The kid at the edge of the playground. The relative who never gets asked a question at dinner. Pick one. Say their name to yourself, if you know it. If you don't, notice that. Picture their face as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can hold them before the God who sees. The bell holds the time.
El Roi, the God who sees: the name Hagar, a runaway slave in the desert, gives to God by a spring. Today's word.
Your line: thou god who seest me. Today, learn the name of one person you see often but have never really looked at, and use it. Day three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic social teaching speaks of God hearing the cry of the poor and of a special care for those pushed to the margins.

fork.setup: you're Hagar, pregnant and alone by a spring in the desert. a messenger of the Lord has called you by name and promised you a son. what do you do?
options: give God a name: the God who sees me.
ask the messenger to bring Sarai.
fork.reveal: she names God: "Thou the God who hast seen me." the well is named after it too.

original.note: Hebrew: El Roi, God of seeing, the God who sees me. Hagar's name for God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a side story about Abraham's household.
what it means: the person nobody in the camp looks at is seen, named and heard, and she names God back.
what a scholar hears: El Roi, and Ishmael, God hears; in Genesis 16, the one who names God is an Egyptian slave woman.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 16:8 and 16:13 quoted from memory; confirm wording. The carry ('thou god who seest me') follows the index and the KJV-like wording; the script quotes the Douay-Rheims form.
'First person in the Bible to give God a name' follows the index; confirm (Genesis 16:13).
'Abram and Sarai never once say her name' in chapter 16: in 16:1–6 the narrator names her but Sarai and Abram refer to 'my handmaid/thy handmaid'. Confirm.
'Ten years' (16:3). Custom of surrogate wives: attested in ancient Near Eastern texts; stated as 'the custom of the time allowed'. Confirm.
The well (16:14) named Beer-lahai-roi ('the well of him that liveth and seeth me' in the Douay-Rheims); paraphrased.
Return-and-submit instruction (16:9) acknowledged plainly; confirm the handling is appropriate.

Editor review (days 333-350): removed the superlative 'first person in the Bible to give God a name' everywhere (hook line, teach, word, myth, fork, trapdoor), since Genesis 16 does not say it; a Keeper may restore it if the index requires. The ten years (16:3) are now ten years in Canaan, not 'the promise of a child is ten years old'; cut 'the custom of the time allowed', 'slave girl', 'many parishes' and 'the Church has long held up'.
